metadata.title: Lesekompetenzen von Grundschulkindern in Deutschland im internationalen Vergleich (IGLU 2011)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses IEA’s complex survey sampling design with a two-stage stratified cluster approach (schools sampled first, then classes within schools). To correct for unequal selection probabilities and nonresponse, the report states that statistical weights are computed for each tested student and then used when calculating statistics such as means and percentages. For uncertainty estimation, standard errors are computed using Jackknife repeated replication (JRR), which is appropriate for clustered designs and avoids underestimation of sampling error. Because this is an IEA/PIRLS/IGLU scaling and reporting framework rather than an ML prediction pipeline, the manuscript does not provide a single named student weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly describes the use of sampling weights and JRR replicate procedures in the estimation of standard errors and significance testing.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report describes the Plausible Values (PVs) approach for scaling achievement (five PVs drawn and combined using multiple imputation logic), but it does not document a specific missing-data handling strategy for questionnaire or item nonresponse at the student level. This is a reporting gap for missingness handling transparency: while PVs address missingness in the achievement measurement context, the manuscript does not specify whether questionnaire missingness was handled via listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation. Therefore, missing_data_handling is set to not_reported for this extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is the German IGLU 2011 target population at the end of Grade 4 (fourth year of formal schooling; age criterion applied internationally). In Germany, the initial school sample was reduced from 200 to 198 schools (excluding an international school with English as instruction and a non-compulsory private school). Performance testing was planned in 197 schools; testing was aborted at one special-needs school, leaving 197 schools. Of 4,229 students in the 197 schools, 4,000 students participated in the IGLU reading test; non-participation (229) is attributed to exclusion reasons, leaving school before the test day, or absence on the test day. The report also requires minimum participation thresholds for scaling interpretability (e.g., at least 85% student participation within schools/classes and at least 85% school participation), and it excludes cases with non-scalable performance values (footnote system indicates a minimum of sufficient items and at least one successfully solved task for scaling).

data.outcome_summary: This IGLU 2011 volume reports international and national results for reading literacy at the end of Grade 4, using IEA’s PIRLS/IGLU framework. Achievement is scaled with IRT (3-PL) and PVs: five plausible values are drawn per student and combined using multiple-imputation logic (Rubin-style combining), enabling comparisons across rotated test booklets. Germany’s reported analytic participation is about 4,000 students from 197 schools, selected via a two-stage stratified cluster design; sampling weights and Jackknife repeated replication (JRR) are used to compute standard errors and significance. On the overall reading scale, Germany’s mean is 541 points, significantly above the international mean (512) and above the EU comparison group (534), and comparable to the OECD mean (538). The report also benchmarks competence levels (e.g., 9.5% at the highest level V; 15.4% below level III) and shows that the 2006 improvement was not sustained by 2011, with 2011 roughly matching 2001. Limitations for causal interpretation are inherent: the study is descriptive/monitoring rather than an ML causal design, and questionnaire missing-data handling is not fully specified in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is for an IEA/Waxmann reporting volume and its methodological description of IGLU 2011 (sampling, scaling, PVs, weighting, and competence levels), not for an empirical ML prediction study. The manuscript does not train or evaluate machine-learning models with predictive targets; instead it uses psychometric scaling (IRT) and multiple-imputation PV procedures for achievement reporting. Consequently, ML technique fields and structured ML findings are intentionally left empty, while the assessment design and PV/weighting logic are captured in the survey_design and outcome_summary.
